title: Scientific Writing, Citations, and Using Credible Sources
text:
Overview
Biology is a scientific discipline grounded in observation, experimentation, and evidence-based reasoning. Scientific knowledge does not exist in isolation; it builds upon the work of other researchers. As a result, scientists must evaluate credible sources, cite prior work properly, and communicate findings clearly and accurately.
In this course, you will learn how to:

Ask scientific, testable questions
Identify and evaluate credible biological sources
Properly cite scientific literature
Communicate findings using accepted formats of scientific writing

Together, these skills form the foundation of scientific literacy and integrity.

Avoiding Plagiarism
Plagiarism is the act of presenting another person’s work, ideas, words, or creative output as your own without giving proper credit to the original source. This can include copying text directly, paraphrasing someone else’s ideas without acknowledgment, or submitting work that was created by someone else, such as a classmate or an online source. Plagiarism is considered a serious academic and ethical violation because it misrepresents authorship, undermines intellectual honesty, and deprives the original creator of recognition for their work.

Use your own words
Cite all non-original ideas
Keep accurate research notes
Use quotes sparingly in science

Writing for Science
Scientific writing emphasizes clarity, precision, and conciseness to ensure that ideas and findings are communicated effectively. Clarity means presenting information in a straightforward and understandable manner, avoiding ambiguity or unnecessary complexity. Precision involves using specific, accurate language and terminology so that the meaning is exact and scientifically correct. Conciseness requires eliminating unnecessary words or repetition, allowing the reader to quickly grasp the essential information without distraction. Together, these principles help make scientific communication efficient, credible, and accessible to other researchers.

Structure of a Scientific Paper
The structure of a scientific paper provides a standardized format that allows researchers to communicate findings clearly and logically. Each section has a specific purpose: the Introduction presents background and the research question, the Methods describe how the study was conducted, the Results report the data, and the Discussion interprets the findings. This organized approach helps readers quickly understand the study and evaluate its validity.

text:
Summary and Application to Laboratory Work
This chapter introduces the foundational skills required for success in biology, emphasizing the importance of scientific thinking, credible research, proper citation, and effective communication. Biology relies on evidence-based investigation, meaning that students must be able to ask testable scientific questions, evaluate reliable sources, and interpret data accurately. Understanding how to distinguish between scientific and non-scientific questions ensures that laboratory work remains focused on measurable and reproducible outcomes.
A key component of scientific work is the use of credible sources, particularly scholarly and peer-reviewed materials. Students learn to differentiate between primary and secondary sources and to evaluate credibility using criteria such as the CRAAP test. This ensures that conclusions are based on accurate, unbiased, and scientifically valid information.
Equally important is the ethical use of information. Proper citation practices allow students to give credit to original researchers, avoid plagiarism, and strengthen the credibility of their work. Using consistent citation formats such as APA or CSE helps maintain professional standards in scientific communication.
The chapter also introduces scientific writing, which prioritizes clarity, precision, and conciseness. Students learn the standard structure of a scientific paper—including Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion—and the purpose of each section. This structure ensures that experiments can be clearly understood, evaluated, and replicated.

title: 1  Laboratory Safety and Measurement
text:
1.1 Introduction: Laboratory Safety and Measurement
Welcome to your first biology lab! Before you begin conducting experiments, it is essential to learn how to work safely and accurately in a laboratory setting. This lab will introduce you to the basic skills and habits that scientists use every day.
In the first part of this lab, you will learn about laboratory safety. Even in an introductory biology lab, there are potential hazards such as chemicals, glassware, biological materials, and heat sources. Understanding how to recognize these risks—and how to respond to them—helps protecting you, your classmates, and your experiments. Following safety rules also ensure that your results are reliable and free from contamination. These safety practices are not only important in class but are also essential in real-world careers such as healthcare, research, and biotechnology.
In the second part of this lab, you will focus on scientific measurement, which is a key skill in all areas of science. You will learn how to use the metric (SI) system, the standard system used by scientists worldwide. You will practice measuring length, mass, and volume using common laboratory tools such as rulers, balances, graduated cylinders, and pipettes. You will also learn how to convert between units, record data correctly, and organize your results.
Finally, you will explore how scientists evaluate data by learning the difference between accuracy (how close a measurement is to the true value) and precision (how consistent repeated measurements are). You will also practice calculating percent error and displaying your data using graphs.
Together, these skills—working safely, measuring carefully, and recording data accurately—form the foundation for all future lab work. Mastering them now will help you succeed in this course and prepare you for more advanced scientific investigations.
Laboratory Safety and Measurement Objectives
By the end of this laboratory unit, students will be able to:

D. Data and Scientific Reasoning

Differentiate between accuracy and precision and evaluate measurements based on these concepts.
Analyze measurement error and identify potential sources of error in laboratory procedures.


E. Professional and Scientific Practice

Explain how laboratory safety practices translate to real-world careers in healthcare, research, and biotechnology.

Perform conversions between metric units using the following prefixes: k-, d-, c-, m- and µ-.

Background:
Scientists use scientific methods to understand the natural world. An important aspect of the scientific process is collecting and analyzing data from observations and experiments. Two methods of measuring and recording data have been commonly used - the Imperial and the Metric System. The Imperial System uses units such as inches and pounds while the Metric System, a decimal-based system, uses units such as meters, liters, and grams. Because of its ease of use, the metric system is more widely used within the modern scientific community. The universal “language” of modern science is based on the metric system and learning to use it is the main purpose of this lab.
Part 1: Introduction to Metric System
Work conducted in science laboratories requires a functional understanding of the metric system, which serves as the standard system of measurement in scientific research. The metric system employs standardized, decimal-based units to measure length, mass, and volume, ensuring that measurements are precise, reproducible, and universally interpretable. Appropriate laboratory instruments are selected based on the quantity being measured; for example, balances are used to measure mass in grams, and graduated cylinders are used to measure liquid volume in milliliters.
The metric system is built upon a set of base units commonly used in biology. The meter (m) is the standard unit for measuring length; the liter (L) is used to measure volume, and the gram (g) is used to measure mass. Temperature in biological laboratories is typically measured in degrees Celsius (°C). All recorded measurements must include both a numerical value and the proper unit. For example, a measurement of 2 m indicates a length that is twice the base unit of length, the meter. Standard unit symbols and abbreviations are allowed and should be used consistently when recording data.
A primary advantage of the metric system is the ease with which units can be converted. Because the system is based on powers of ten, conversions involve multiplication or division by 10 or multiples of 10. For example, one decameter is equal to ten meters, and one kilometer is equal to one thousand meters. This base ten structure simplifies calculations, reduces the likelihood of errors, and makes the metric system especially well-suited for scientific measurements and laboratory applications.

Reading a Meniscus
When measuring liquid volume in a pipette or graduated cylinder, it is important to read the meniscus, the curved surface of the liquid. Most liquids (like water) form a concave meniscus, meaning the surface curves downward.
To obtain a correct measurement:

Position your eyes level with the liquid surface to avoid parallax errors.
Read the measurement at the lowest point of the meniscus (the bottom of the curve) for those liquids that form a concave meniscus. For liquids that form a convex meniscus (such as mercury), the measurement should be read at the top of the curve.
Ensure the instrument is upright on a flat surface, and the liquid is still.

Lab Activity 1.7: Accuracy and Precision
When making measurements, both precision and accuracy are extremely important. Precision of a measurement refers to the closeness of repeated measurements or the reproducibility of the measurement. Precision can be affected by the measuring instrument. If a student uses a thermometer calibrated to the nearest degree to measure the temperature of a beaker of water and a second student uses a thermometer that is calibrated to the nearest ten degrees for the same exercise, the reproducibility or precision of measurements will be greater for the student using the thermometer calibrated to the nearest degree. The thermometer with the greatest number of calibrations (smallest increments) is the most precise, and thus the reproducibility is greater. Accuracy, described as how close a measurement is to its true value, however, is dependent upon both the precision of the measuring instrument and the technical skills of the individual taking the measurement. title: 2  Use of the Microscope
text:
2.1 Introduction: Use of the Microscope
In this lab, you will learn how to use one of the most important tools in biology: the compound light microscope. Microscopes allow scientists to observe objects that are too small to be seen with the naked eye, such as cells, tissues, and microorganisms. Learning how to effectively use a microscope is a fundamental skill that you will use throughout this course and in many scientific careers.
During this lab, you will become familiar with the parts of the microscope and how each part works together to produce a clear image. You will focus on specimens using different magnifications, starting with low power, and working your way up to higher magnifications. As you increase magnification, you will notice critical changes in what you see, including how much of the specimen is visible (field of view) and how much of it stays in focus (depth of field).
You will also learn how to prepare your own slides using a technique called a wet mount, which allows you to see living or freshly prepared specimens. In addition, you will practice making careful observations and recording what you see through drawings and notes—an essential part of scientific investigation.
Proper handling and care of the microscope will be emphasized throughout the lab. Using the microscope correctly not only protects delicate equipment but also ensures that your observations are accurate and reliable.
By the end of this lab, you will have the skills needed to confidently use a microscope to explore the microscopic world and better understand the structure of living organisms.

2.13 Introduction: Magnification and Microscope Use
This laboratory activity introduces students to the proper use of the compound light microscope, a fundamental tool in biological sciences. Students will learn to identify microscope components, understand how magnification is achieved, and develop skills in focusing on specimens at increasing levels of magnification. Emphasis will be placed on proper handling, accurate observation, and the relationship between magnification, field of view, and depth of field. Mastery of these techniques is essential for examining biological specimens and conducting accurate scientific observations.

2.17 Focusing on Specimens
For biology 110 labs you will only be focusing on a total magnification of 400x. You will have to use the oil immersion lenses (1000x) in your Microbiology (230) classes. For your first practical, you will have to focus clearly on a specimen at a total magnification of 400x. You will have two minutes to complete this task.
Focusing on a specimen may be broken down into a three-step process.

Scanning Lens (4x):


Begin focusing on a specimen using the Scanning lens. First, adjust the mechanical stage so that it is at its lowest position. You can do this by turning the course focus knobs away from your body.
Turn on the light. And adjust the ocular lenses so that your field of view is a circle of light.
Place and center the specimen on the mechanical stage.
Look into the oculars and slowly raise the mechanical stage by turning the course focus knob towards your body. Stop when it comes to focus. You may adjust the focus using the fine focus knob that is needed.
Center the specimen. Adjust the X-Y stage knobs so that your specimen is in the center of your field of view. This position will enable you to see the specimen when you adjust the lens to the next higher magnification. If the specimen is found to the side, then you may lose the specimen from your field of view when you adjust your objective lens to the next higher magnification.


Low Power (10x)

Next, while looking into your objective lenses, turn the turret clockwise (to the right) to 10x power.
Adjust the focus. Do not use the course focus knob to adjust your focus. Only use the fine focus knob at this point. If you use the course focus knob, then you may adjust your focus too far out of focus and may have to start at the Scanning power again.
Center your specimen

High Power (40X)

Finally, switch to the high-power lens (40X) by turning the lens to the right (clockwise). At this point only use the fine focus to adjust the focus.
If the color of light is too yellow, you may adjust the rheostat to change the color of light to a white light.
If the light is too dark, you may adjust the diaphragm.

2.18 Measuring and Calculating the Field of View
The field of view is the area of the specimen you can see through the ocular lenses. When you adjust your magnification, the diameter will decrease at higher magnifications. The image below, figure 2.3, is an example of a field of view.
How to find the field of view:

Obtain a prepared slide with a ruler and place it on the stage.
Adjust the ruler so that the edge of the ruler is visible as a series of tic marks/lines that lie across the diameter or the field of view as in the figure below.




https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Field_of_view_diameter_in_microscopy.jpg/1024px-Field_of_view_diameter_in_microscopy.jpg


Microscope field of view showing a metric ruler aligned across the circular viewing area, with measurement markings used to determine the diameter of the field of view.
Figure 2.3. Field of view diameter being measured in a microscope with a metric ruler. Mikael Häggström, 29 January 2020. CC0.
Arrange the slide so that the horizontal line is aligned along the midline of the field as seen above. Align one of the vertical lines so that it is at the edge of your field of view, as you can see on the right side of the picture. The space between the leading edge of the horizontal lines is 1 mm in distance, see the yellow bar.

Measure the distance of the field of view for the scanning lens (4X)

________________ mm.
________________ µm

Measure the distance of the field of view for the low power lens (10x)

__________ mm
__________ µm


When you use high-power and oil-immersion lenses, you should not be able to measure the field of view directly. At this point, you will have to calculate the field of view. This calculation is a simple conversion using the formula below:
Conversion Formula:
(Diameter of the field; A) X (Total Magnification: A) = (Diameter of the field; B) X (Total Magnification: B)
In this case “A” stands for the known field information of the measured field of view of either the scanning or low-power magnification and “B” stands for the information of the new or unknown lens magnification (e.g., high-power or the oil immersion lenses)

Figure out the distance of the field of view for the high-power objective lens (40X)

________________ mm.
________________ µm




Determine the distance of the field of view for the oil-immersion objective lens (100X)

__________ mm
__________ µm

Center the “e” and look at it through the oculars. Draw this “e” and label it.

Field of View and Depth of Field of a Microscope


When viewing a specimen through a microscope, the visible area appears circular and is referred to as the field of view. The diameter of this circle decreases as magnification increases.



Circular microscope field of view displaying the prothallium of Polypodium vulgare at 4× magnification, showing a thin, flat, green plant structure centered within the viewing area.
Figure 2.4. Circular microscope field of view showing the prothallium (prothallus) of Polypodium vulgare. Taken with a light microscope on x4 magnification. Image: Viséan, 2019, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org

Circular microscope field of view displaying an unknown plant specimen, showing cellular or tissue structures within a round viewing area under magnification.
Figure 2.5. A view of an unknown plant under a microscope. Palmer-Harris, L. (2021, December 28).CC BY SA 4.0.


The depth of field is the vertical distance (top to bottom) within the specimen that stays in focus at one time. As magnification increases, the depth of the field decreases. Therefore, the scanning objective lens provides the greatest depth of field, while the oil immersion objective lens has the shallowest depth of field.


Microscopic view showing three overlapping yarn fibers at 40× magnification, with only portions of the fibers in sharp focus at a time, illustrating limited depth of field.
Figure 2.6. View showing three overlapping yarn fibers (40×). Image from Botweb, the University of Wisconsin, https://botweb.uwsp.edu/130y.htm.

A prepared slide having three differently colored silk fibers or threads is commonly used to show depth of field. In this preparation, the threads are arranged to cross at a single point, with each thread positioned at a different vertical level. By focusing at 400x and adjusting the fine focus and seeing which thread comes into focus first, second, and last, the relative positions of the threads—top, middle, and bottom—can be figured out.

2.20 Preparing a Wet Mount
You will have to prepare wet mount slides of fresh specimens on many occasions during this course. You will often need to apply a biological stain to a specimen to see the structures within cells. Such stains combine with cellular components. Selective use of available stains enables the observer to see desired components. It is also important when preparing wet mount slides to use the thinnest section of a specimen possible. You will use a scalpel or razor blade to section your specimens. A wet mount requires a layer of liquid to completely fill the space between the slide and coverslip, immersing the specimen and enabling the observer to clearly focus through the microscope.

title: 2  Use of the Microscope
text:
2.21 Procedure:

Wet mount of an Onion Skin


Watch the video on this link to see how to prepare wet mount of an onion skin and then follow the instructions below:


Prepare the specimen


Peel a small, rectangular piece of transparent epidermis (inner layer) from a sliced onion.
Place the onion skin flat in the center of a clean glass slide.


Stain


Add one drop of methylene blue directly onto the onion skin.
Let it sit for 1 to 2 minutes, so the stain penetrates the cells.


Remove excess stain and rinse


Gently touch a corner of a paper napkin to the slide edge (not the specimen) to wick away excess stain.
Add one small drop of water to rinse the stained area, then wick away the rinse with the napkin.
Repeat the rinse once, if needed, remove the excess each time.


Mount with a coverslip


Place one final small drop of water on the specimen.
Hold the coverslip at a 45° angle and slowly lower it onto the drop to spread the liquid and avoid air bubbles.


A student lowers a coverslip at a 45-degree angle onto a glass slide having a drop of liquid and a specimen, allowing the liquid to spread evenly and prevent air bubbles from forming beneath the coverslip.
Figure 2.7 Image of placing a coverslip on a glass slide when making a wet mount. Image courtesy of New York City College of Technology. BY CC NC SA 3.0.

Clean slide edges


Run the edge of a paper napkin around the coverslip to remove excess fluid.
Wipe and dry the bottom of the slide so it is clean for viewing.


Observe under the microscope


Secure the slide on the stage. Start with the scanning objective lens (4X) to find tissue; center a clear area in the field of view.
Switch to low power (10X), re-center and refocus, then move to high power (40X) for details (40X objective with a 10X eyepiece = 400X).
Always center and refocus before increasing magnification. Draw or image what you see.


Finish and dispose


Rotate the scanning (4X) objective lens into place and lower the stage. Remove the slide and place it in the “Used Slides” container.
Clean and store equipment per lab protocol and wash your hands.


Safety notes: avoid pressing the coverslip, handle methylene blue carefully, and follow your lab’s disposal procedures.


Wet mount of human cheek cells

Watch the video on this link to see how to prepare wet mount of a cheek cell and then follow the instructions below:

Wash your hands with soap and water.
Watch the onionskin wet mount video first.
Use a sterile cotton swab or the flat end of a clean toothpick to gently scrape the inside of your cheek (do not poke or scrape hard).
Place a clean microscope slide on a flat surface and add one drop of water to the center.
Rub the swab or toothpick tip gently through the drop for ~4 seconds to transfer cells. Discard the used swab/toothpick safely.
Add one drop of methylene blue to the smear (at the edge of the drop to avoid bubbles).
Carefully lower a cover slip at an angle over the drop to avoid trapping air bubbles.
Blot any excess stain from the slide edge with absorbent paper.
Place the slide on the microscope stage. Start with the scanning (4X) lens to locate the sample, then switch to a 40X objective (400X total with a 10X eyepiece) to observe stained cheek cells.
When finished, dispose of the cover slip and slide per your lab’s biohazard or sharps protocol, and wash your hands.

Safety notes: wear gloves and eye protection if available; avoid swallowing stains; do not reuse contaminated toothpicks; follow institutional disposal rules.

text:
2.22 II. Wet Mount Preparation of Cultured Organisms and Pond Water
View the instructional video in this link to review wet mount preparation techniques using cultured organisms. Then complete the following procedure.

Gather materials: plastic pipette, clean slide, coverslip, and your sample (cultured organisms or pond water).
Use the pipette to draw liquid from near the bottom of the container (where organisms collect).
Put 1 or 2 drops of the sample in the center of the slide.
Hold the coverslip at a 45° angle and slowly lower it onto the drop to avoid air bubbles.
Blot excess liquid by touching a paper napkin to the coverslip edge; dry the underside of the slide.
Place the slide on the stage. Start with the 4× (scanning) objective lens to find the specimen, center it, then move to 10× and 40×—recenter and refocus at each step.
Record observations with a labeled drawing.
Finish: return the 4× objective lens, lower the stage, remove the slide, and put it in the “Used Slides” container.

Safety: avoid contaminating the sample, do not a pipette by mouth, and follow lab disposal rules.

title: 2  Use of the Microscope
text:
2.23 End-of-Lab Procedures

Clean and return all prepared slides to their designated storage trays.
Turn off and unplug the microscope; neatly wrap the power cord around the cord holder or base.
Rotate the head to face inward toward the microscope body.
Set the objective turret to the scanning (4×) objective lens.
Lower the stage fully.
Place the dust cover over the microscope (if available).
Return the microscope to its assigned storage cabinet.

Troubleshooting Guide

Image too dark


Check power: ensure the microscope is plugged in and switched on; confirm the light is lit.
Increase light: raise the rheostat (brightness control).
Open the iris diaphragm and/or raise the condenser to let more light through.
Fine-tune the rheostat until the image is bright and white.


Unable to see a single image with both eyes


Move your head slightly away from the eyepieces.
Adjust interpupillary distance by sliding the oculars together or apart until one image appears.


Stationary spot in the field of view


The lens is likely to be dirty. Use only lens paper to gently clean the oculars and objective lenses.
If needed, carefully remove the ocular to clean the inner surface.
Do not use tissues, paper towels, or clothing (they can scratch lenses).


Eyelashes or other near eye artifacts visible


e too close to the eyepieces—move your head back a little.


Nothing visible at high power


Always focus on scanning (4×) and low (10×) first, center the specimen, then switch to high (40×).
Make sure the specimen is centered before increasing magnification.


Only part of the field is illuminated (half-moon)


Ensure the objective clicks fully into place on the nosepiece.
Adjust the condenser and its centering to align the light.


Image stays blurry and will not focus


Check the slide orientation (not upside down) and that it is secured in the stage clips.
Recenter the specimen and refocus at lower magnification before switching up.


Eye strain or headache from using the microscope


Focus first with your dominant eye (e.g., right eye), then adjust the other ocular diopter.
Set interpupillary distance correctly and reduce light intensity if it is too bright.
Take short breaks to rest your eyes.

Quick maintenance/reminders

Always start with the lowest magnification, center the specimen, then increase power.
Use only lens paper for optics.
If problems persist, notify the instructor or lab technician.

This table provides key terminology related to microscopy, along with concise definitions of each term. It serves as a reference for understanding the structure, function, and proper use of the microscope, as well as concepts such as magnification, and resolution.








Chapter 2: Microscopy Glossary







Terms


Definitions




binocular


a microscope having two eyepieces




brightfield microscope,


a compound microscope with two or more lenses that produce a dark image on a bright background.




coarse focusing knob


used for large-scale movements with 4⨯ and 10⨯ objective lenses




condenser lens


(located below the stage), which focuses all the light rays on the specimen to maximize illumination.




fine focusing knob


used for small-scale movements, especially with 40⨯ or 100⨯ objective lenses.




fixation


The process of attaching cells to a slide.




illuminator


provides light for the brightfield microscope




lens


a medium with a curved surface that refracts and focuses on light to produce an image.




magnification


the ability of a lens to enlarge the image of an object when compared to the real object




monocular microscope


a microscope having a single ocular lens




objective lenses


the lenses far end of the body tube




ocular lens


the eyepiece of a microscope




oil immersion lens,


a special lens designed to be used with immersion oils.




refraction


occurs when light waves change speed and direction as they pass from one medium to another.




resolution


The ability to tell that two separate points or objects are separate.




rotating nosepiece, also known as the revolving turret,


sits below the head of the microscope and locks the objective lens into position over the stage aperture by rotating in either direction.




stage


(a platform) of the microscope total magnification is the product of the ocular magnification times the objective




Total magnification


(ocular magnification × objective magnification)




wet mount


slide preparation in which the specimen is placed on the slide in a drop of liquid.




x-y mechanical stage knobs.


These knobs move the slide on the surface of the stage, but do not raise or lower the stage.

3.2 Introduction: Molecules, Water, and pH

Biology is the study of life, and understanding life begins with understanding the chemistry that makes it possible. In this first-semester biology lab, you will explore the fundamental chemical principles that underlie biological systems, preparing you for advanced work as a biology major or pre-med student. Through hands-on experiments and model-based activities, you will connect basic chemical concepts to real biological function.
Chemical compounds can be divided into two broad categories: inorganic and organic. Inorganic compounds, such as water, salts, acids, and bases, generally do not contain carbon–hydrogen (C–H) bonds and play essential roles in maintaining life processes. Organic molecules, on the other hand, are defined by the presence of carbon and C–H bonds. Carbon’s unique ability to form four covalent bonds allows it to create a wide variety of complex molecules, especially when combined with other key elements such as oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur—elements that make up the vast majority of living matter.
In this lab, you will investigate how atoms form molecules through covalent bonding, where electrons are shared between atoms. You will learn how to represent molecules using molecular formulas, structural formulas, and abbreviated structural formulas, each providing different levels of detail. Using molecular model kits, you will build three-dimensional representations of molecules to better understand how atomic arrangement influences molecular shape and function. You will also explore isomers, which are molecules with the same molecular formula but different structures, demonstrating how small differences in arrangement can lead to significant biological differences.
A major focus of this lab is water, one of the most important inorganic molecules for life. Because of its polar structure, water exhibits unique properties such as cohesion, adhesion, high surface tension, and high specific heat. These properties allow water to act as a solvent, regulate temperature, and move through narrow spaces via capillary action—all essential for sustaining life. You will perform experiments to observe and measure these properties directly.
You will also examine acids, bases, and pH, which are critical for maintaining proper conditions in biological systems. The pH scale measures the concentration of hydrogen ions in a solution and determines whether a solution is acidic, neutral, or basic. Because the pH scale is logarithmic, even small changes represent significant shifts in chemical conditions. Living systems depend on tightly regulated pH levels—for example, human blood must remain within a narrow range to support proper enzyme and cellular function. To maintain this balance, organisms rely on buffers, which resist changes in pH when acids or bases are introduced.
By combining theory with experimentation, this lab will help you develop essential scientific skills, including observation, data collection, analysis, and critical thinking. These foundational concepts will support your future studies in biology, chemistry, and medicine, and provide insight into how chemical processes sustain life at every level.

title: 4  Chemical Composition of Cells
text:
4.3 Introduction
All living organisms are composed of chemical compounds that perform essential functions needed for life. The majority of these compounds belong to four major classes of biological macromolecules:

Carbohydrates
Proteins
Lipids
Nucleic acids

In this laboratory exercise, you will examine three of these macromolecules—carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids—using chemical indicator tests. These tests allow scientists to identify specific types of molecules based on observable color changes or staining patterns. Although these laboratory tests do not determine the exact concentration of a substance, they provide valuable information about whether a particular biological molecule is present in a sample.

title: 4  Chemical Composition of Cells
text:
4.4 Carbohydrates
Carbohydrates are organic molecules composed primarily of carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and oxygen (O), generally in a ratio of approximately 1:2:1.
They serve several important biological functions including:

Immediate energy source
Energy storage
Structural support
Cell recognition

Carbohydrates are classified according to the number of sugar units they contain.

4.4.1 Monosaccharides
Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates because they consist of a single sugar molecule.
Examples include:

Glucose
Fructose
Galactose

Although glucose, galactose, and fructose all have the same chemical formula (C6H12O6), they differ structurally and chemically (and are isomers) because of the different arrangement of functional groups around the asymmetric carbon.
The chemical formula for glucose is C6H12O6. In humans, glucose is an important source of energy. During cellular respiration, energy is released from glucose, and that energy helps make adenosine triphosphate (ATP). 
Galactose (part of lactose, or milk sugar) and fructose (found in sucrose, in fruit) are other common monosaccharides.
Monosaccharides are considered reducing sugars, meaning they possess a free aldehyde or ketone group capable of reducing certain chemical reagents such as Benedict's reagent.

Disaccharides are formed when two monosaccharides join together through a dehydration synthesis reaction, creating a glycosidic bond.
Examples include:

4.4.3 Polysaccharides
Polysaccharides consist of hundreds or thousands of monosaccharides linked together.
Major examples include:

4.4.3.1 Starch

Plant energy storage molecules
Composed of glucose
Digestible by humans



4.4.3.2 Glycogen

Animal energy storage molecules
Highly branched

4.4.3.3 Cellulose

Structural component of plant cell walls
Humans cannot digest cellulose because we lack cellulase

Unlike monosaccharides, polysaccharides are generally not reducing sugars.

title: 4  Chemical Composition of Cells
text:
4.5 Proteins
Proteins are large biological molecules composed of amino acids linked together by peptide bonds.
Proteins perform a tremendous variety of cellular functions including:

Enzymes
Structural support
Transport
Hormones
Cell signaling
Immune defense
Muscle contraction

Protein function depends upon its unique three-dimensional structure.

4.5.1 Amino Acids
Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.
Each amino acid contains:

Amino group (-NH₂)
Carboxyl group (-COOH)
Hydrogen atom
Variable R-group (side chain)

Twenty different amino acids are commonly used to construct proteins.
Differences in their side chains determine the chemical properties and function of proteins.

title: 4  Chemical Composition of Cells
text:
4.6 Lipids
Lipids are hydrophobic molecules composed primarily of carbon and hydrogen.
Unlike carbohydrates, lipids contain relatively little oxygen.
Major functions include:

Long-term energy storage
Cell membrane structure
Hormone production
Thermal insulation
Cushioning organs

Common classes of lipids include:

Fats
Oils
Phospholipids
Steroids
Waxes


4.6.1 Fatty Acids
Most fats consist of glycerol attached to three fatty acids forming triglycerides.
Fatty acids differ in the presence or absence of double bonds.

4.6.1.1 Saturated Fatty Acids
Saturated fatty acids contain only single carbon-carbon bonds.
Characteristics:

Straight hydrocarbon chains
Pack tightly together
Usually solid at room temperature

Examples:

Butter
Lard
Coconut oil

Excessive dietary intake is associated with increased cardiovascular disease risk.


4.6.1.2 Unsaturated Fatty Acids
Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds.
These double bonds introduce bends (kinks) into the fatty acid chain.
Characteristics:

Do not pack tightly
Usually liquid at room temperature

Examples:

Olive oil
Canola oil
Fish oil

Unsaturated fats are generally considered healthier dietary fats.

4.7 Qualitative versus Quantitative Tests
Scientists use different laboratory methods depending on the information they need.

4.7.1 Qualitative Tests
Qualitative tests determine whether a substance is present or absent.
Results are based on observations such as:

Color change
Precipitate formation
Layer formation
Staining

Example:
Benedict's test indicates whether reducing sugars are present.
This laboratory uses qualitative testing.


4.7.2 Quantitative Tests
Quantitative tests determine how much of a substance is present.
Results are numerical and often require specialized equipment such as:

Spectrophotometers
Colorimeters
Analytical balances

Examples include:

Blood glucose measurements
Protein concentration assays
Cholesterol analysis

title: 4  Chemical Composition of Cells
text:
4.8 Experimental Controls
Controls are essential components of every scientific experiment because they ensure that results are reliable and meaningful.

4.8.1 Positive Control
A positive control contains a substance known to produce the expected positive result.
Example:
Glucose solution serves as the positive control for Benedict's test because glucose is reducing sugar.
A successful positive control confirms that:

The reagent is functioning properly
The procedure was performed correctly



4.8.2 Negative Control
Negative control lacks the substance being tested.
Distilled water is commonly used.
Negative control should produce no reaction.
It confirms that:

Positive results are due to the sample rather than contamination or reagent error.

4.9.5 Part IV. Sudan III Test for Lipids
Principle
The Sudan III test is a qualitative test used to detect the presence of lipids (fats and oils). Sudan III is a fat-soluble dye that dissolves in lipids rather than water. When lipids are present on filter paper, the dye is retained in the lipid-containing area, producing a red to orange-red stained spot.
Materials

Filter paper
Pencil
Forceps
Cotton swabs
Sudan III solution
Distilled water (negative control)
Vegetable oil (positive control)
Test samples
Petri dish or staining tray

Procedure

Place a piece of filter paper in a clean Petri dish or on a clean surface.
Using a pencil, draw and label circles (approximately 1–2 cm in diameter) for each sample.
Add 1–2 drops of each sample into its designated circle using cotton swabs.
Include:


1. Positive control (Vegetable oil)
2. Negative control (Distilled water)
3. Coconut milk (juice)
4. Whole milk
5. Skim milk
6. Italian dressing
6. Fat-free Italian dressing
7. Unknown


Allow the samples to air dry completely (approximately 10–15 minutes).
Pour enough Sudan III solution into a Petri dish to cover the filter paper.
Place the dried filter paper into the Sudan III solution for 3–5 minutes.
Remove the filter paper using forceps.
Rinse gently with distilled water for about 30–60 seconds to remove excess stain.
Use a blow dryer to dry filter paper briefly.
Observe and record the color of each spot, record results in table.

4.9.8 Scientific Significance
Chemical indicator tests provide a rapid method for identifying biological molecules in foods, biological samples, and laboratory specimens. These qualitative assays are widely used in biology, biochemistry, medicine, food science, microbiology, and environmental science. Understanding how these tests work reinforces the relationship between molecular structure and biological function while introducing students to the principles of experimental design, including the use of controls, observation, and data interpretation. This laboratory also emphasizes that while qualitative tests identify the presence of a molecule, quantitative methods are required to accurately measure its concentration in research and clinical settings.

5.1 Introduction: Molecular Structure of Biological Molecules
Carbohydrates, Lipids, Proteins, Nucleic Acids, and Functional Groups
Estimated Time: 2.5–3 hours
Living organisms are composed of many organic molecules, most of which can be grouped into four major biological classes: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids. These molecules are central to life because they store energy, provide structural support, regulate cellular processes, form membranes, catalyze reactions, and carry genetic information.
Many biological molecules are built from smaller units. For example, simple sugars called monosaccharides may exist as individual molecules or join to form disaccharides and polysaccharides. Amino acids link together to form polypeptides and proteins. Nucleotides form nucleic acids such as DNA and RNA. Lipids are more chemically diverse; some contain fatty acids and glycerol, while others, such as sterols, contain fused carbon rings.
In this laboratory, you will examine molecular models and structural formulas representing the four major classes of biological molecules. You will identify functional groups, compare molecular structures, and relate structure to biological functions. As you work, focus on how atoms, bonds, polarity, molecular shape, and subunit arrangement influence what each molecule does in living systems.

A. Monosaccharides: Glucose
Glucose is a six-carbon monosaccharide with the molecular formula: C6H12O6

6.2 Introduction: Molecular Movement in the Cells and Across Cell Membranes

All cells are enclosed by membranes which provide a semi-permeable barrier between the internal contents of the cell and its external environment. Cells must be able to regulate the movement of molecules or ions (i.e., amino acids, sugars, O2) so that their concentrations do not disrupt cell metabolic processes. In addition to regulating what contents may enter or exit the cell, the cell membrane plays a role in a few other functions, including communication, binding, and adhering to adjacent cells. Properties of the cell membrane can be determined by exposing red blood cells to different solutions (i.e., different “environments”) and observing the appearance of cells under a microscope. The cell may, for example, lyse due to the influx of water. More specifically, we will be looking at how animal cells (red blood cells) and plant cells respond differently to distinct types of solutions.
Diffusion

Molecules can pass a cell membrane using different means of transport. One such means is passive transport; in which case the laws of thermodynamics dictate the flow of molecules. In passive transport, no added energy (ATP) is necessary for the movement of molecules as they move along their concentration gradient, passing from high to low concentration. There are several types of passive transport, including diffusion and osmosis.
Some, but not all, of the traffic across the membranes of cells occurs by diffusion. Diffusion is the movement of molecules from an area of greater to an area of lesser concentration. Molecules are in motion constantly due to their natural movement caused by thermal agitation (Brownian Motion), and they bounce off each other and disperse themselves in an area until equilibrium is reached. Equilibrium means that the molecules have an equal distribution across the medium. Keep in mind that each particle is exhibiting random motion— you cannot predict which way an individual particle will move—but you can predict the net movement of the collection of particles.
As biological membranes are selectively permeable, some substances can freely diffuse through the membrane more easily than others. This is due to the contrasting properties of the phospholipid bilayer that makes up the cell membrane, as it includes both polar and nonpolar regions. Moreover, substances that move through the membrane can do so at different rates. Hydrophobic or non-polar molecules, such as hydrocarbons, oxygen, and carbon dioxide, can dissolve in the membrane and cross it with ease due to the hydrophobic nature of the membrane. Conversely, most hydrophilic molecules, such as ions and polar molecules, cannot pass through the membrane.
Osmosis
Osmosis is a special case of passive transport that deals with the diffusion of water across a selectively permeable membrane. Osmosis depends upon the concentration of solutes in a solution. A solution is made up of a solvent, the substance that does the dissolving, and a solute, the substance that is being dissolved. In the case of osmosis, the solvent is water. A Solute is a substance, such as sugar or salt that is dissolved in the water.
In comparing two solutions of unequal solute concentration, the solution with a greater concentration of solutes is said to be hypertonic. The solution with the lesser solute concentration is hypotonic. These are relative terms that are only meaningful in a comparative sense. For example, tap water is hypertonic to distilled water, but hypotonic to seawater. In other words, tap water has a higher concentration of solutes than distilled water, but a lower concentration than seawater. Solutions of equal solute concentration are said to be isotonic.
If a cell is placed in an environment which is isotonic, an environment of equal solute concentration, then there is no concentration gradient. Without such a gradient, there will be no net flow of water across the membrane.
If a cell is placed in a hypotonic environment, then there is a lower solute concentration surrounding the cell than within the cell. Whenever the solute concentration is lower, the concentration of free water molecules is higher. Therefore, water will diffuse alongdown its concentration gradient from an area of higher concentration (outside the cell) to an area of lower concentration (inside the cell). The added pressure that develops because osmosis is occurring is called hydrostatic (or turgor) pressure. This pressure may increase the point of opposing the entry of more water by osmosis (in which case it is equal to osmotic pressure), or this pressure may cause the membrane to rupture before such a point is reached.
Conversely, a cell placed in a hypertonic environment is surrounded by solution which is higher in solutes, hence lower in free water molecules. In this case, the free water concentration is greater inside the cell than outside, so the water flows out of the cell.
Plant and animal cells will respond differently in hypertonic, hypotonic, and isotonic solutions. This is primarily due to the presence of a cell wall in plant cells, which is absent from animal cells. For example, an animal cell (such as a red blood cell) will lyse (burst open) in a hypotonic solution due to the movement of water molecules into the cell. A plant cell placed into a hypotonic solution is considered turgid, however, and will not lyse due to the presence of the cell wall.

6.5 Appendix: Key Terms and Definitions for the Osmosis and the Cell Lab







Term
Definition




Active Transport
The movement of substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, requiring energy (ATP).


ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate)
The primary energy-carrying molecule used by cells to power processes such as active transport.


Brownian Motion
The random movement of particles in a fluid is caused by collisions with other fast-moving molecules.


Cell Membrane
A selectively permeable barrier composed of a phospholipid bilayer that regulates what enters and exits the cell.


Cell Wall
A rigid outer layer found in plant cells that provides structure and prevents over-expansion during water uptake.


Centrioles 
Cylindrical structures involved in organizing microtubules and assisting in cell division in animal cells. 


Chromatin 
A complex of DNA and proteins (histones) that form chromosomes and help regulate gene expression. 


Chromosomes 
Threadlike structures made of DNA that carry genetic information, especially visible during cell division. 


Cilia 
Short, hair-like structures that move fluid or substances across the cell surface. 


Concentration Gradient
The difference in the concentration of a substance between two areas.


Cytoplasm (cytosol) 
The gel-like substance inside the cell where organelles are suspended and many metabolic reactions occur. 


Cytoskeleton 
A network of protein filaments that provides structural support, shape, and movement for the cell. 


Dialysis Tubing
A semi-permeable membrane used in experiments to model how substances move across cell membranes.


Diffusion
The passive movement of molecules from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.


Equilibrium
A state in which molecules are evenly distributed, resulting in no net movement.


Flagellum 
A long, whip-like structure that enables cell movement (e.g., sperm cell motility). 


Golgi apparatus 
An organelle that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for transport. 


Hypertonic Solution
A solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell, causing water to move out of the cell.


Hypotonic Solution
A solution with a lower solute concentration than the cell, causing water to move into the cell.


Isotonic Solution
A solution with equal solute concentration inside and outside the cell, resulting in no net water movement.


Lysosome 
A membrane-bound organelle containing digestive enzymes that break down waste materials and cellular debris. 


Mass Change
A measurable increase or decrease in mass used to determine water movement during osmosis experiments.


Microvilli 
Small, finger-like projections that increase surface area for absorption, commonly found in intestinal cells. 


Mitochondria 
Organelles that generate energy (ATP) through cellular respiration; often called the cell’s 'powerhouse.' 


Nucleus 
A membrane-bound organelle that contains the cell’s DNA and controls cellular activities. 


Nuclear envelope 
A double membrane that surrounds the nucleus, containing pores that regulate material exchange. 


Nucleolus 
A dense region within the nucleus where ribosomal RNA (rRNA) is produced, and ribosome assembly begins. 


Osmosis
The passive movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from an area of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration.


Passive Transport
The movement of substances across a membrane without the use of cellular energy, following the concentration gradient.


Peroxisome 
An organelle containing enzymes that break down fatty acids and detoxify harmful substances using oxygen. 


Phospholipid Bilayer
The double layer of phospholipids that forms the basic structure of the cell membrane, with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails.


Red Blood Cells
Animal cells are often used in experiments to observe membrane behavior in different solutions.


Ribosome 
A small organelle responsible for protein synthesis, found free in the cytosol or attached to rough ER. 


Rough endoplasmic reticulum 
A membrane network studded with ribosomes involved in protein synthesis and folding. 


Selective Permeability
The property of a membrane that allows some substances to pass while restricting others.


Smooth endoplasmic reticulum 
A membrane network without ribosomes involved in lipid synthesis and detoxification. 


Solute
A substance that is dissolved in a solution.


Solvent
The substance (often water) that dissolves the solute to form a solution.


Transport Mechanism
Any process that allows substances to move across the cell membrane (e.g., diffusion, osmosis, active transport).


Turgor Pressure
The pressure exerted by water inside a plant cell against the cell wall, helping maintain structure.

7.3 Introduction
As you have learned in the lecture part of this course, enzymes are protein molecules that catalyze various reactions in living organisms. They allow organisms to carry out complex chemical activities at relatively low temperatures and are highly specific for one or a group of related reactions. Enzymes bring substrates together in a manner that increases the likelihood that a reaction will occur. One of the unique features of enzyme-catalyzed reactions is that enzymes are not consumed during the process. That is, enzymes stay unchanged during the reaction and can be reused repeatedly.
Many factors can affect enzyme activity, and in this laboratory, we will study the effects of substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, temperature, pH, and inhibitors on enzyme activity (Pitkin, 1992).
In this series of experiments, you will use enzyme peroxidase isolated from turnips. Peroxidases catalyze the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. In reactions catalyzed by peroxidase, reducing agents, such as guaiacol, donate electrons and hydrogen atoms, while hydrogen peroxide acts as the oxidizing agent. These reactions result in the formation of water and an oxidized organic compound, tetraguaiacol, as shown in the equation below:
4 H₂O₂ + 4 guaiacol → tetraguaiacol + 4 H₂O
Guaiacol acts as the hydrogen donor (i.e., it is the reducing agent). When guaiacol is oxidized, it changes from a colorless liquid to a dark orange-brown compound (tetraguaiacol). In this experiment, blue light (470 nm) will be passed through the solution, and a colorimeter will measure the amount of light transmitted. This measurement is based on the absorption of blue light by the brown-colored solution (Enzyme Activity Guided Inquiry Lab: Turnip Peroxidase, 2018).

title: 8  Respiration and Yeast Fermentation
text:
8.1 Introduction: Respiration and Yeast Fermentation
All living organisms need energy to survive. Plants and animals take energy from the environment and convert it into forms their cells can use. In plants, this begins with photosynthesis, where light energy from the sun is converted into chemical energy stored in glucose. This stored energy then becomes available to living cells through cellular respiration, a series of metabolic pathways that break down glucose and convert its energy into ATP, the usable form of energy for cellular work.
Sugars such as glucose are especially important because they have a large amount of energy stored in their chemical bonds. In organisms that use oxygen, cellular respiration is essentially the reverse of photosynthesis. In this process, glucose reacts with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water, and energy:
C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O
During aerobic respiration, oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain, allowing cells to produce a large amount of ATP using energy carried by molecules such as NADH and FADH₂.
But when oxygen is unavailable, cells must use alternative pathways to keep producing energy. In these anaerobic conditions, cells rely on fermentation to regenerate NAD⁺ from NADH so that glycolysis can continue producing ATP. Fermentation uses organic molecules as final electron acceptors and does not require oxygen.
There are two common types of fermentation. Lactic acid fermentation occurs in animal muscle cells during intense exercise and in certain bacteria; it converts pyruvate into lactic acid while regenerating NAD⁺:
C₆H₁₂O₆ → Pyruvic acid + NADH ↔︎ lactic acid + NAD⁺
Alcohol fermentation, used by yeast, converts pyruvate into ethanol and carbon dioxide while also regenerating NAD⁺:
C₆H₁₂O₆ → Pyruvic acid → CO₂ + acetaldehyde → ethanol
Yeast are single-celled eukaryotic fungi that are widely used in industry to produce bread, beer, wine, and various chemicals. In this lab, you will investigate how yeast carry out alcohol fermentation and produce carbon dioxide (CO₂) while breaking down sugars for energy.
During cellular respiration, yeast metabolize sugars and release CO₂ as a byproduct. You will test three monosaccharides—glucose, fructose, and galactose—which all share the same chemical formula (C₆H₁₂O₆) but differ in structure as isomers.
You will also examine two disaccharides, lactose and sucrose, which have the same chemical formula (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁) but different molecular arrangements.
Sucrose Lactose Maltose
By comparing how yeast ferments these different sugars, you will see how molecular structure influences the rate and efficiency of fermentation. Overall, this experiment will help you understand how cells generate energy under anaerobic conditions through processes such as fermentation.

title: 10  Mendelian Genetics in Corn and Chi-Square Testing
text:
10.2 Introduction: Corn Genetics
Genetics is the study of how traits are passed from parents to offspring. In this lab, you will explore these ideas using corn (Zea mays). Corn is a useful organism for studying genetics because each ear contains many kernels, and each kernel represents one offspring. These kernels clearly show visible traits, such as color (purple or yellow) and shape (round or wrinkled), making patterns of inheritance easier to observe.
Traits are controlled by genes, which are located on chromosomes. For each gene, organisms inherit two copies, called alleles—one from each parent. These alleles can be the same (homozygous) or different (heterozygous). The combination of alleles is called the genotype, while the physical appearance of the trait is the phenotype.
Some alleles are dominant, meaning they are expressed even if only one copy is present. Others are recessive, meaning they are only seen when two copies are present. For example, in corn, purple color is typically dominant over yellow, and round shape is dominant over wrinkled. Even if a recessive trait is not visible in one generation, it can reappear in later generations.
The principles you will use in this lab were first described by Gregor Mendel. His Law of Segregation states that allele pairs separate during the formation of gametes, so each gamete carries only one allele. His Law of Independent Assortment states that different genes are inherited independently, as long as they are on different chromosomes.
You will begin by using Punnett squares to predict the expected ratios of traits in offspring. In a monohybrid cross (one trait), the expected phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation is usually 3:1 (dominant to recessive). In a dihybrid cross (two traits), the expected ratio is typically 9:3:3:1.
However, real data rarely matches these ratios exactly. To test whether your results fit Mendelian predictions, you will use a chi-square (χ²) test. This statistical method helps determine whether differences between your observed data and expected values are due to random chance or suggest a different pattern of inheritance.
By the end of this lab, you will connect genetic theory to real data and develop skills in scientific reasoning, data analysis, and interpretation—important tools for all areas of biology.
The research question is: Does simple Mendelian inheritance explain the color and shape of corn seeds?
If the answer is yes, then you are assuming that:

Each trait is controlled by two alleles that show complete dominance.
Each trait is determined by a single gene.
In the dihybrid cross, the genes for these traits are located on different chromosomes and assort independently.
The data you collected are accurate, meaning the seeds were counted, and their traits were identified correctly.

Monohybrid cross
In this cross, the first-generation parents were homozygous for a single trait, e.g., either PP for purple (dominant) or pp for yellow (recessive). The offspring of this cross is the F1 generation, all of which are the same genotype.

Chi-Square in Genetics
In genetics, Punnett squares are used to predict the expected ratios of traits in offspring. However, real experimental data rarely match these predictions exactly. Slight differences between expected and observed results are common due to chance, sampling variation, or experimental error.
The chi-square (χ²) test is a statistical method used to decide whether the differences between observed and expected results are significant, or simply due to random variation.
The chi-square test compares:

What you observed in an experiment
What you expected based on a genetic hypothesis

This allows you to evaluate whether your data fits the expected genetic model.
Key idea:
The chi-square test helps determine whether deviations from expected ratios are due to chance or show a different genetic outcome.
Chi-Square Formula
χ2=∑[(O−E)2] / E
Where:

O = observed value
E = expected value
Σ = sum of all data points

Using Chi-Square in a Monohybrid Cross
Example: 3:1 Phenotypic Ratio
Step 1: State Hypothesis
The observed results follow a 3:1 ratio (dominant: recessive).
Step 2: Observed Data

Tall = 78
Short = 22

Step 3: Expected Values

Tall = 75
Short = 25

Step 4: Calculate Chi-Square
χ2=∑[(O−E)2] / E
χ2= [(78−75)2+(22−25)2 ] = 9 + 9 = 0.12 + 0.36 = 0.48
75 25 25 25

Step 5: Degrees of Freedom
Degrees of freedom (df) represent the number of independent categories that can vary when calculating a chi-square value.
In genetics chi-square problems, degrees of freedom are calculated using the formula:
df=number of categories−1
Examples

Monohybrid cross (2 categories: dominant and recessive):

df=2−1=1

Dihybrid cross (4 categories: 9:3:3:1):

df=4−1=3

Why It Matters
The degrees of freedom determine which value you use from the chi-square table. This allows you to decide whether the difference between observed and expected results is significant.

Step 6: Interpretation
Compare χ² (0.48) to critical value (3.84 at p = 0.05, df = 1)
Since: 0.48<3.84

Why 3.84 is the Critical Value for a population of two observations
The number 3.84 comes from a chi-square distribution table and represents a cutoff point based on:


Degrees of freedom (df = 1)
Significance level (p = 0.05)

A graph of the Chi-squared distribution can be seen in figure 11.1.

This is the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is true (a false positive).
A p-value of 0.05 means that there is a 5% chance that any difference between the observed and expected results is due to random chance. This sets out a cutoff point for deciding whether the result is significant.
For a chi-square test with 1 degree of freedom, this cutoff value (called the critical value) is 3.84.
So:


If your χ² value is less than 3.84, the difference is due to chance (not significant).
If your χ² value is greater than 3.84, the difference is unlikely due to chance (significant).

That 5% region is called the rejection region.
On the graph, our calculated Chi-squared value of 0.48 is far left of 3.84.

A vertical line marks the critical value at 3.84 on the right side of the graph. The calculated chi-square value (0.48) is found far to the left of this line, in the high-probability region, showing that the result is not significant.

title: 11  Introduction to Mendelian Genetics
text:
11.1 Introduction
Gregor Mendel is widely recognized as the father of modern genetics because his experiments provided the first clear explanation of how inherited characteristics are transmitted from one generation to the next. Mendel was born in 1822 and grew up on a farm, where he developed an early interest in plants. His later education in mathematics and science, especially at the University of Vienna, helped him apply quantitative reasoning to biological questions.
Between 1856 and 1865, Mendel conducted controlled breeding experiments using pea plants (Pisum sativum). He selected pea plants because they possessed easily observed traits, reproduced quickly, and could be artificially fertilized under controlled conditions. By tracking characteristics such as seed shape, seed color, flower color, and plant height across generations, he demonstrated that traits are inherited as discrete hereditary units rather than blending together. These findings became the conceptual basis for what are now called genes.
Mendel presented his results to the Natural History Society of Brno in 1865 and published them in 1866 in a paper titled Experiments in Plant Hybridization. Despite the importance of his conclusions, the work attracted little attention at the time. Historians and science references note that his paper circulated only narrowly and that many contemporary scientists did not appreciate the significance of his mathematical treatment of inheritance. Mendel’s work was not widely recognized until about 1900, when other scientists rediscovered similar inheritance patterns and connected them to his earlier publication.
The modern language of genetics emerged after Mendel, but the principles he discovered remain foundational. A gene is a unit of heredity, and a trait is a heritable characteristic influenced by one or more genes. Alternative versions of a gene are called alleles, and the specific physical position of a gene on a chromosome is its locus. Diploid organisms inherit two alleles for most genes, one from each parent. When both alleles are the same, the organism is homozygous for that gene; when the alleles differ, the organism is heterozygous.
The outward expression of a genetic characteristic is the phenotype, whereas the underlying allele combination is the genotype. In classical Mendelian inheritance, a dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype whenever it is present, while a recessive allele is expressed only when two recessive copies are inherited. However, not all inheritance patterns follow simple dominance. In incomplete dominance, the heterozygous phenotype is intermediate between the two homozygous phenotypes. In codominance, both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote. In sex-linked inheritance, the gene responsible for a trait is located on a sex chromosome, most often the X chromosome.
In this laboratory, students will first analyze a monohybrid cross, which follows the inheritance of a single trait. Monohybrid crosses are especially useful for examining complete dominance, incomplete dominance, codominance, and sex-linked traits. Students will then examine a dihybrid cross, which tracks two traits simultaneously and illustrates how genes may assort independently during gamete formation. Together, these exercises introduce the predictive framework of Mendelian genetics.
Objectives
Upon completion of this laboratory exercise, students should be able to:

11.3 Monohybrid Cross Problems Using a Punnett Square
A monohybrid cross follows the inheritance of a single gene or trait. In a Punnett square, the possible gametes from one parent are written across the top, and the possible gametes from the other parent are written along the side. Each box inside the square represents one possible offspring genotype. This allows students to predict both genotypic ratios and phenotypic ratios for a cross.
For a trait that follows complete dominance, the dominant allele is expressed whenever it is present, while the recessive allele is expressed only when an individual has two recessive copies.
Problem 1: Worked Example: Homozygous Dominant × Homozygous Recessive
In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white flowers (p*). Cross a homozygous dominant purple-flowered plant with a homozygous recessive white-flowered plant.

Parent 1 genotype = PP
Parent 2 genotype = p*p*

Step 1. Determine the gametes from each parent
Because each gamete receives only one allele for the gene, the PP parent can produce only P gametes, and the p*p* parent can produce only p* gametes. This follows Mendel’s principle of segregation.

Gametes from PP: _____, _____
Gametes from p*p*: _____, _____

Step 2. Set up the Punnett square
Fill in the outer boxes below


Step 3. Identify the offspring genotypes
All four boxes contain the genotype Pp*.

Offspring genotypes: 100% Pp*
Genotypic ratio: 0 PP : 4 Pp* : 0 p*p*
Simplified genotypic ratio: 100% heterozygous

Step 4. Identify the offspring phenotypes
Because P is dominant, every offspring with genotype Pp* will have purple flowers. In complete dominance, a heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype.

Offspring phenotypes: 100% purple flowers
Phenotypic ratio: 4 purple : 0 white

Conclusion
A cross between a homozygous dominant parent and a homozygous recessive parent produces offspring that are:

100% heterozygous
100% dominant phenotype

This is a useful first example because every offspring has the same genotype and the same phenotype.

text:
11.4 Extensions of Monohybrid Crosses
Not all inherited traits follow the simple dominant–recessive pattern first described by Mendel in pea plants. Although Mendel’s work established the basic principles of segregation and inheritance, later studies demonstrated that some traits exhibit alternative inheritance patterns, including codominance, incomplete dominance, and sex-linked inheritance. These patterns can still be analyzed using the same general approach as a standard monohybrid cross, but the relationship between genotype and phenotype differs from that seen in complete dominance. [Experiment...gor Mendel], [en.wikipedia.org]
In the following sections, you will examine three important extensions of Mendelian inheritance. For each pattern, you should determine the parental genotypes, identify the possible gametes, construct a Punnett square, and then predict both the genotypic and phenotypic outcomes of the cross. Although the Punnett square method remains the same, interpretation of the offspring changes depending on the dominance relationship between the alleles or on whether the gene is carried on an autosome or a sex chromosome.

11.4.1 Monohybrid Crosses with Codominance
In codominance, both alleles in a heterozygous individual are fully and distinctly expressed in the phenotype; one allele does not mask the other. A classic biological example is the ABO blood group system, in which the Iᴬ and Iᴮ alleles are codominant and are both expressed in individuals with genotype IᴬIᴮ, producing blood type AB. Allele i, when it appears, is recessive and is masked by either IA or IB. In laboratory exercises, codominance is often illustrated with coat-color traits in animals, such as red and white coat alleles in cattle, where the heterozygote displays both red and white hairs.
Solved Example: Codominance
In cattle, red coat color (Cᴿ) and white coat color (Cᵂ) are codominant. A heterozygous animal with genotype CᴿCᵂ has a roan coat, meaning that both red and white hairs are visible. Cross two roan cattle.

Phenotypic ratio: 1 red : 2 roan : 1 white
This example illustrates that, in codominance, the heterozygote has a phenotype in which both alleles are visibly expressed, rather than one allele masking the other or producing an intermediate blend.

11.4.2 Monohybrid Crosses with Sex Linkage
A sex-linked trait is determined by a gene located on a sex chromosome, most commonly the X chromosome. In humans and many other organisms, females typically have two X chromosomes (XX) and males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). Because males have only one X chromosome, they possess only a single copy of most X-linked genes and will express a recessive X-linked allele whenever it is present. Females generally must inherit two recessive alleles to express a recessive X-linked trait. As a result, X-linked recessive conditions often occur more frequently in males than in females.
A common instructional example is red–green color blindness, which is usually treated as an X-linked recessive trait. In this notation, Xᴺ represents the normal-vision allele and Xⁿ represents the color-blind allele; the Y chromosome does not carry a corresponding allele for this trait.

11.4.3 Monohybrid Crosses with Incomplete Dominance
In incomplete dominance, neither allele is completely dominant over the other, and the heterozygote displays an intermediate phenotype between the two homozygotes. This pattern differs from codominance because the heterozygote does not show both traits distinctly; instead, it shows a phenotype that appears blended or intermediate. A classic example is snapdragon flower color, in which red-flowered plants and white-flowered plants produce pink-flowered heterozygous offspring.
A commonly used notation for this trait is:

CᴿCᴿ = red
CᵂCᵂ = white
CᴿCᵂ = pink

11.4.4 Comparative Summary
These three types of monohybrid crosses illustrate that not all single-gene traits follow complete dominance. In codominance, both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygote. In incomplete dominance, neither allele is fully dominant, and the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype. In sex-linked inheritance, the pattern of transmission depends on whether the gene is located on a sex chromosome and whether the offspring is male or female. Despite these differences, each pattern can still be analyzed using the same stepwise process of identifying parental genotypes, determining gametes, constructing a Punnett square, and interpreting the resulting genotypic and phenotypic ratios., https://courses.lumenlearning.com/suny-oneonta-osbiology2e-1/chapter/characteristics-and-traits/

text:
11.5 Dihybrid Crosses
A dihybrid cross is a genetic cross that examines the inheritance of two different traits (two genes) simultaneously. While a monohybrid cross follows one trait, a dihybrid cross allows us to observe how alleles of different genes are inherited together and whether they assort independently. This concept reflects Mendel’s principle of independent assortment, which states that alleles of different genes are distributed independently into gametes (provided the genes are not linked).
In a dihybrid cross, each parent contributes two alleles for each of two genes, and each gamete receives one allele from each gene. As a result, more combinations of gametes are possible compared to a monohybrid cross.
Using FOIL to Determine Gametes
To solve dihybrid crosses efficiently, students can use the FOIL method, a technique adapted from algebra:

First
Outer
Inner
Last

This method helps determine all possible gamete combinations from a heterozygous individual.
Example:
For a genotype AaBb, apply FOIL:

First: A B → AB
Outer: A b → Ab*
Inner: a B → a*B
Last: a b → a*b*

Thus, this individual produces four types of gametes:

AB, Ab*, a*B, a*b*

Practice Problems: Dihybrid Crosses
Simple Problem 1

More Advanced Problems
Challenge Problem 1
In plants:

Tall (T) is dominant to short (t*)

Challenge Problem 2
In mice:

Challenge Problem 3

Challenge Problem 4
In corn:

Yellow kernels (Y) are dominant to white (y*)

Smooth white
Wrinkled yellow
Wrinkled white

Explain how the data supports your answer
Draw the appropriate Punnett square

Challenge Problem 5

50% show both recessive traits

No mixed phenotypes appear.
Questions:

Summary
Dihybrid crosses extend the principles learned in monohybrid crosses by examining two traits simultaneously. The use of the FOIL method simplifies the process of determining gametes, and Punnett squares allow prediction of offspring outcomes. When both parents are heterozygous and genes assort independently, the expected phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1, but deviations from this ratio can reveal additional biological insights such as linkage or test crosses.

11.6 Key Terms / Glossary
Trait – A heritable characteristic or feature of an organism, such as flower color or seed shape.
Gene – A basic unit of heredity that contributes to a specific biological characteristic.
Locus – The specific location of a gene on a chromosome.
Allele – One of two or more alternative versions of a gene at a given locus.
Homozygous – Having two identical alleles for a gene.
Heterozygous – Having two different alleles for a gene.
Dominant – Refers to an allele that is expressed in the phenotype when present in a heterozygous individual.
Recessive – Refers to an allele whose effect is masked in a heterozygous individual and expressed only when two recessive alleles are present.
Phenotype – The observable physical or physiological characteristics of an organism.
Genotype – The allele combination or genetic constitution of an organism.
Monohybrid Cross – A genetic cross that tracks the inheritance of a single trait or gene.
Dihybrid Cross – A genetic cross that tracks the inheritance of two different traits or genes at the same time.
Complete Dominance – A pattern of inheritance in which the heterozygote has the same phenotype as the homozygous dominant individual.
Incomplete Dominance – A pattern of inheritance in which the heterozygous phenotype is intermediate between the two homozygous phenotypes.
Codominance – A pattern of inheritance in which both alleles are fully expressed in the heterozygous phenotype.
Sex-Linked Inheritance – Inheritance of traits determined by genes located on the sex chromosomes, commonly the X chromosome.

text:
11.8 Procedure Overview
Part I. Review of Mendelian Terminology and Genetic Notation

Review the definitions of the terms provided in the glossary.
Practice writing genotypes using standard letter notation for dominant and recessive alleles.
Distinguish between genotype and phenotype for several sample organisms or traits.

Part II. Monohybrid Crosses with Complete Dominance

Examine a genetic trait controlled by two alleles in which one allele is completely dominant to the other.
Construct Punnett squares for parental crosses provided by the instructor or laboratory handout.
Determine the expected genotypic and phenotypic ratios for the offspring.
Compare predicted ratios with any observed class or sample data, if provided.

Part III. Monohybrid Crosses with Incomplete Dominance

Analyze a trait in which the heterozygous phenotype is intermediate between the two homozygous phenotypes.
Use Punnett square analysis to predict offspring genotypes and phenotypes.
Record expected ratios and compare them with complete dominance outcomes.

Part IV. Monohybrid Crosses with Codominance

Examine a trait in which both alleles are expressed in the heterozygous condition.
Complete Punnett square analysis for the assigned codominant cross.
Compare the resulting phenotypic ratios with those seen in complete and incomplete dominance.

Part V. Monohybrid Crosses with Sex Linkage

Review the inheritance of a trait controlled by a gene located on the X chromosome.
Use sex-linked notation to represent parental genotypes.
Predict the expected phenotypic distribution among male and female offspring.
Identify why reciprocal crosses may produce different results in sex-linked inheritance.

Part VI. Dihybrid Crosses

Construct Punnett squares or use a forked-line method to analyze a cross involving two separately inherited traits.
Determine the expected genotypic and phenotypic ratios.
Evaluate how the results illustrate Mendel’s principle of independent assortment.

Part VII. Interpretation and Discussion

Summarize the inheritance pattern observed in each type of cross.
Compare different modes of inheritance and identify how they alter expected phenotypic ratios.
Answer post-laboratory questions using both calculations and written explanations.
